title: Separation and divorce in BC: how your taxes and benefits change
seo_title: Separation and Divorce: Tax and Benefit Changes in BC (2026)
description: Separating or divorcing in BC? Learn the CRA's 90-day rule, how your benefits change, how child and spousal support are taxed, and how to split property.
lead: A separation changes a lot more than your living arrangements. It changes your marital status for tax purposes, the benefits you receive, how support payments are taxed and how your shared property and savings can be divided. Getting the tax side right early can protect your benefit payments and save you from a bill later. Here is a plain-language overview for people in British Columbia.
key_points: For tax purposes, you count as separated once you have lived apart because of a relationship breakdown for at least 90 days.
After the 90 days, tell the CRA by the end of the month after your status changed so your benefits are recalculated correctly.
Child support under an order or agreement made after April 1997 is not taxable or deductible; spousal support usually is.
Register any order or agreement that includes spousal support with the CRA on Form T1158.
RRSP and TFSA savings can move to a former partner without tax if done as a direct transfer under a court order or written agreement.
If neither parent can agree who claims the eligible dependant amount for a child, neither parent can claim it.

sections.heading: When does the CRA treat you as separated?
sections.html:
Your marital status is how the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) describes your relationship on your tax return: married, living common-law, separated, divorced, widowed or single. It matters because many credits and benefits are based on your family net income, which is your income plus your partner's.

A common-law partner is someone you live with in a marriage-like relationship who is not your legal spouse. For tax purposes, that usually means you have lived together for 12 months in a row, or you share a child by birth or adoption.

The 90-day rule

  • You are separated when you have lived apart from your spouse or common-law partner because your relationship broke down, for at least 90 days.
  • Once you reach 90 days, your separation counts from the first day you lived apart, not from day 90.
  • Living apart for other reasons, such as work, school, health or time in prison, does not make you separated.
  • You are divorced only once the divorce is legally final. Until then, a married person who has lived apart for 90 days is separated.

Illustration: Sam and Alex stop living together on March 1 because their relationship has ended. They are still apart on May 30, 90 days later, so the CRA treats them as separated from March 1.

B.C. family law uses a different test

Tax rules and family law rules are not the same. Under B.C.'s Family Law Act, unmarried partners must have lived together in a marriage-like relationship for at least two years before the property and debt division rules apply. A couple with a child together can qualify for spousal support with less time than that.

sections.heading: Telling the CRA about your new status
sections.html:
• Wait for the 90 days. Do not report a separation until you have been apart for at least 90 days.
  • Then report it quickly. The CRA asks you to report a change by the end of the month after the month your status changed.
  • How to report: update your status in CRA My Account (the fastest way), call the CRA's benefits line at 1-800-387-1193, or mail Form RC65, Marital Status Change.
  • If you already filed: if you filed as a couple before reaching 90 days apart, and you then stay apart past 90 days, update your status and file a change (an amended return) to fix amounts you claimed as a couple.

Reporting on time matters. Your benefits are recalculated on your new family income, and late reporting can lead to overpayments that you have to pay back.

Both of you should keep filing a tax return every year, even with no income. The CRA needs each return to work out benefits such as the Canada child benefit.

If you are leaving an abusive situation: the CRA says you do not need your partner's signature on any benefit form, and you never need to contact an abusive person to get your benefits. If you can't get the usual documents, a letter from a shelter or a copy of a police report can be used instead. You can update your address right away, without waiting 90 days.

sections.heading: How your benefits change
sections.html:
Canada child benefit (CCB)

The CCB is a tax-free monthly payment for families with children under 18. After a separation is reported, the CRA recalculates it using your new status and your own family income. The new amount starts with the month after the month your status changed.

  • Only one parent in a household gets the CCB for a child. When a child lives with a mother, the CRA usually treats her as the parent mainly responsible for the child. If the other parent is actually mainly responsible, they can apply with a signed letter from the mother saying so.
  • Shared custody means the child lives with each parent about equally, which the CRA treats as 40% to 60% of the time with each. In that case, each parent gets half of what they would get if the child lived with them full-time.
  • Each parent should tell the CRA about a new custody arrangement right away, through My Account or Form RC66.

Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (formerly the GST/HST credit)

In July 2026, the GST/HST credit was renamed the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit. It is a tax-free payment, made four times a year, for people with low or modest incomes. After a separation, each of you is assessed separately from the date you started living apart, and the CRA sends a notice showing the new amount. In shared custody, each eligible parent may get half of the amount for the child.

B.C. family benefit

The B.C. family benefit is a provincial payment for families with children under 18. The CRA pays it with your CCB in one monthly deposit, using the same application, so you do not apply separately. The CRA lists a separate amount for the first child in a single-parent family (up to $41.66 a month for July 2026 to June 2027), so your payment can change when you become a single parent. Our CCB and B.C. family benefit guide explains how the amounts are worked out.

sections.heading: Child support and spousal support: who pays tax?
sections.html:
Support payments are regular amounts one person pays to help support a former partner, their children, or both. Child support is for the children. Spousal support is only for the former spouse or common-law partner. For the CRA to treat a payment as support, it generally must be:

  • set out in a court order or written agreement, with a specific amount;
  • paid on a periodic (regular) schedule, such as monthly, as the order or agreement sets out;
  • paid while you live apart because the relationship broke down (for a former partner); and
  • money the recipient can use however they choose.
Child supportSpousal support
Order or agreement made after April 1997Not deductible for the payer and not taxable for the recipientUsually deductible for the payer and taxable for the recipient
Payer reports it onLine 21999 (total paid)Line 21999 (total) and line 22000 (deductible part)
Recipient reports it onLine 12799 (total received)Line 12799 (total) and line 12800 (taxable part)
Register with the CRA?Not if the order covers child support onlyYes, on Form T1158

Older orders and agreements made before May 1997 can follow the old rules, where child support is also taxable and deductible. That changes if the child support amount was later changed, or if both parents sign Form T1157 to move to the newer rules, a choice that can't be undone.

Rules that catch people out

  • Spousal support counts only if child support is fully paid. When an order covers both, payments are applied to child support first. Spousal support is deductible only when all child support owed for the year and earlier years has been paid.
  • Payments before the paperwork. Support paid before the order or agreement is signed, in the same year or the year before, counts only if the order or agreement says so.
  • Register spousal support. Send Form T1158 for each order or agreement that includes spousal support. Do not attach the agreement to your return, but keep proof of every payment, such as bank statements or cancelled cheques.

Illustration: Jordan pays $1,000 a month in child support and $500 a month in spousal support under a 2026 separation agreement. Over a full year Jordan would report $18,000 on line 21999 and deduct $6,000 on line 22000. Her former partner reports $18,000 on line 12799 and $6,000 on line 12800.

Warning about lump sums: a one-time payment is usually not support for tax purposes, even if the agreement calls it deductible. A lump sum paid to settle future support is neither deductible nor taxable. Paying overdue support in one amount is treated differently. Get advice before agreeing to a lump sum.

sections.heading: The eligible dependant credit and legal fees
sections.html:
Amount for an eligible dependant (line 30400)

This non-refundable tax credit (a credit that lowers the tax you owe but does not create a refund on its own) can help single parents. A separated or divorced parent may be able to claim it for a child under 18 who lives with them in a home they keep up. Key rules:

  • Only one claim is allowed per household, and the amount can't be split between two people.
  • A parent who must pay child support for a child generally can't claim this amount for that child. The other parent may be able to.
  • If both parents are clearly required to pay support for the same child, or custody is shared, you must agree who claims. If you can't agree, neither of you can claim.
  • Using both parents' incomes to work out child support does not, by itself, mean both are paying.
  • In the year you separate, if you paid support, you can choose either this credit or the deduction for your support payments, whichever helps you more.

Our guide to often-missed tax credits covers other credits single parents should check.

Can you deduct legal fees?

  • Not deductible for anyone: fees to get a separation or divorce, or to set custody or parenting time.
  • Not deductible for the payer: fees to set, fight or reduce support.
  • Deductible for the recipient: fees to collect overdue support, to set the amount of support, or to try to increase it. Fees to try to make child support non-taxable are also deductible.

sections.heading: Dividing property, savings and pension credits
sections.html:
Transfers between partners: the rollover

Normally, when you give away an investment or property that has gone up in value, you pay tax on the capital gain (the increase in value). Between spouses or common-law partners, a special rule called a rollover applies instead. The property moves at its original cost, so there is no tax at the time of the transfer. The person receiving it takes over that original cost and pays the tax when they later sell. You can choose to opt out of the rollover and transfer at market value, but that triggers tax right away.

Attribution rules are anti-income-splitting rules. Normally, if a spouse sells property you gave them, the gain can be taxed back to you. If you are living apart because the relationship broke down, you can file a signed election with your return so the gain is not taxed to you.

RRSPs and TFSAs

  • RRSP: money can move from one partner's RRSP to the other's without tax if it is a direct transfer under a court order or written agreement dividing property, and you are living apart because of the breakdown. The financial institution uses Form T2220.
  • TFSA: a direct transfer between institutions under a court order or written separation agreement, while you live apart, does not affect either person's TFSA room. Withdrawing the cash and handing it over is different, and could put the receiving person over their limit.

Your home

The principal residence exemption can remove the capital gain on your home when you sell it. A family unit can only name one home per year. Your spouse or partner stays in your family unit for a year unless, for that whole year, you lived apart under a court-ordered (judicial) separation or a written separation agreement. If you sell, you must report the sale on your return using Form T2091(IND). See our guide to capital gains and selling a home.

CPP credit splitting

The pension credits you each built up in the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) while living together can be split between you. You must have lived together for at least 12 months in a row. Separated married couples and former common-law partners must also have lived apart for at least 12 months in a row. Former common-law partners must apply within 48 months of starting to live apart. Either of you can apply to Service Canada, online or on Form ISP1901. The split is permanent. Our retirement income guide explains CPP in more detail.

sections.heading: Checklist and common mistakes
sections.html:
Checklist

  1. Note the first day you and your partner lived apart.
  2. After 90 days apart, update your marital status in My Account or on Form RC65, by the end of the following month.
  3. Report any new custody arrangement for the CCB right away.
  4. Make sure your support terms are in a written agreement or court order, with clear amounts for child and spousal support.
  5. Register any agreement that includes spousal support on Form T1158.
  6. Keep proof of every support payment.
  7. Agree in writing which parent will claim the eligible dependant amount for each child.
  8. Move RRSP and TFSA money by direct transfer, not by withdrawing it.
  9. Decide how CPP credits will be split and apply to Service Canada.
  10. Keep filing your tax return every year, on time.

Common mistakes

  • Reporting a separation before 90 days, or forgetting to report it at all.
  • Paying "spousal support" without a written agreement, then trying to deduct it.
  • Deducting spousal support while child support is still owing.
  • Both parents claiming the eligible dependant amount for the same child.
  • Cashing out an RRSP to pay a former partner, instead of a tax-free transfer.
  • Trying to deduct the legal costs of getting a divorce.
